1.note: The phrase **In those days** is a way of referring to the time period being described. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At around that time]

1.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ צַ֣ו לְ⁠בֵיתֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה
1.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that you should command regarding your house, for you are dying, and you will not live]

1.q: צַ֣ו לְ⁠בֵיתֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you are dying, and you will not live, command regarding your house]

Here Hezekiah’s **house** could represent: (1) his household affairs. Alternate translation: [Put your affairs in order] or (2) his royal dynasty. Hezekiah lived 15 years after this illness, but his son and successor Manasseh was 12 years old when he became king, indicating that Hezekiah did not have an heir at this time. He would therefore have had to identify someone as his successor. Alternate translation: [Name your successor]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you will surely die from this illness]

3.note: Hezekiah is not suggesting that Yahweh does not **remember** these things and needs to be reminded of them. He is asking Yahweh to take them into consideration. Alternate translation: [consider] or [take into consideration]

Here **walked** is a metaphor for how Hezekiah has conducted his life before Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have lived]

The phrase **to your face** is a way of saying in your presence or under your authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithfully]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s intentions and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in complete devotion]

The phrase ** good in your eyes** means what you consider to be good or what you approve of. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I have done what you consider to be good]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And Hezekiah wept bitterly]

4.note: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh spoke a message to Isaiah. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 15:10. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to Isaiah]

5.q: הָל֞וֹךְ וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔⁠ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ הִנְ⁠נִי֙ יוֹסִ֣ף עַל־יָמֶ֔י⁠ךָ חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה
5.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Yahweh said (level 1). Yahweh is quoting what he wants Isaiah to say to Hezekiah. (level 2). This includes a quotation from Yahweh himself. (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation, in this verse and at the end of the next verse. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

5.q: הָל֞וֹךְ וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔⁠ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ הִנְ⁠נִי֙ יוֹסִ֣ף עַל־יָמֶ֔י⁠ךָ חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה
5.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Go and tell Hezekiah that I, Yahweh, the God of David his father, have heard his prayer and have seen his weeping. I am going to add fifteen years to his life]

Yahweh refers to David as Hezekiah’s **father**, though David was actually his ancestor several generations back. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ancestor]

Yahweh is using **Behold me, one will add** as a common expression of this culture to mean “I am going to add.” Someone using this expression would more commonly say “Behold me, adding.” Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a solemn pronouncement. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expressions in 28:16 and 29:14. Alternate translation: [I am surely going to add]

6.q: וּ⁠מִ⁠כַּ֤ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ אַצִּ֣ילְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֑את וְ⁠גַנּוֹתִ֖י עַל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּֽאת
6.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be quotations within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that I say that I will deliver him and this city from the palm of the king of Assyria, and I will cover over this city]

6.q: וּ⁠מִ⁠כַּ֤ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ אַצִּ֣ילְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֑את
6.note: Here, **palm** represents the power or control of the king of Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will deliver you and this city from the power of the king of Assyria]
See how you translated the similar expression in 37:35. Alternate translation: [And I will protect this city]

8.note: Yahweh is using a common expression of this culture, **Behold me**, to indicate that he is about to do something. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in 37:7. Alternate translation: [I am going to make the shadow return on the stairs]

The phrase **the stairs of Ahaz** describes a structure that King Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, built to track the passage of time. It showed the time of day by the position of the shadow that a pole cast on a series of **steps** below the pole. Such a structure is sometimes called a “shadow clock.” It is similar to what many cultures know as a sundial. If your readers would not be familiar with such a structure, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [on the steps of the shadow clock that King Ahaz had built] or [on the sundial of King Ahaz]

9.q: מִכְתָּ֖ב לְ⁠חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה בַּ⁠חֲלֹת֕⁠וֹ וַ⁠יְחִ֖י מֵ⁠חָלְיֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: What follows in verses 10-20 is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

10.note: Hezekiah is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is the person making the statement. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, Hezekiah, said]

Hezekiah is using **In the quiet of my days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the prime of my life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the prime of my life]

Here Hezekiah is speaking as if **Sheol**, the place of the dead, were a walled city that he would enter through its **gates**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will go to Sheol when I die]

Hezekiah is using the possessive form to describe **gates** that are characterized by belonging to **Sheol**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into the gates that lead to Sheol]

The expression **I am visited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is taking from me]

The implication is that Yahweh is the one who has cut Hezekiah’s life short. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I am being punished by Yahweh]

11.note: Hezekiah is using **I will not see Yah** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will no longer experience Yahweh’s presence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not be in the presence of Yah]

SPEAKER is repeating forms of the name **Yah** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yah, even Yah, in the land of the living]

Hezekiah is using **in the land of the living** as a common expression of the culture to mean “among those who are still alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the living]

Hezekiah is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who live]

12.q: דּוֹרִ֗⁠י נִסַּ֧ע וְ⁠נִגְלָ֛ה מִ⁠נִּ֖י כְּ⁠אֹ֣הֶל רֹעִ֑⁠י
12.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the tent of a shepherd** is taken down and carried away, so Hezekiah’s life is being **removed** from him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My dwelling is removed and carried away from me, just as a shepherd takes down and carries away his tent]

Here Hezekiah is speaking of his life as if it were a **dwelling** that could be removed and carried away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My life] or [My time on earth]

The expression **is removed and carried away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He has removed my dwelling and carried it away from me]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a weaver** rolls up a finished piece of cloth, so Hezekiah’s life has been brought to its end. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as a weaver rolls up a finished piece of cloth, so my life has been brought to its end]

Here Hezekiah is speaking as if his life were a piece of weaving and Yahweh were a weaver who **is cutting** it **off from the loom**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He is cutting my life short]
The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh, whom Hezekiah has not yet named in his song. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is cutting me off from the loom]

Hezekiah is referring to all of the time of his suffering by naming two major components, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the time]

Even though Hezekiah is addressing Yahweh directly, earlier in this verse he spoke of Yahweh in the third person as **He**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate that in a respectful form in the second person, as he does here with **you are finishing me**. Alternate translation: [you are cutting me off from the loom; from day to night, you are finishing me]

Hezekiah is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **you are finishing me**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [you are causing me to die]

13.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** crushes the bones of its prey, so the pain Hezekiah suffers feels as if it were breaking his bones. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a lion crushing the bones of its prey, so he breaks all of my bones]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [so he breaks all of my bones]

Hezekiah is using **all of my bones** to represent his whole body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my whole body]
See how you translated the similar expression in 38:12.
See how you translated the similar expression in 38:12.

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a swallow** or **a crane** chirps, so Hezekiah moans feebly in his suffering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like a swallow or a crane, so I chirp feebly]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a dove** coos, so Hezekiah moans softly in his distress. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I moan softly like a dove]

Here, **My eyes** represents Hezekiah’s looking to heaven for help. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I look with wearied eyes]

Hezekiah is using **to the height** as a common expression of the culture to mean “upward toward heaven.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [upward toward heaven]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **oppression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am oppressed]

Hezekiah is using **give surety for me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be my guarantor” or “take responsibility to protect me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [be my guarantor]

15.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Hezekiah is using the question form to express his helplessness, since there is nothing he can say in response to what Yahweh has done. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he told me of his plan] or [he informed me of what he intended]
The implication is that it is Yahweh who has spoken to Hezekiah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For Yahweh has spoken to me]

Hezekiah is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he has done** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh himself is taking action. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and he, Yahweh himself, has done it]

Here Hezekiah is speaking of how he will live out his remaining years as if it were going to **walk slowly**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will live humbly all of my years]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bitterness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my bitter soul]

16.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

In this difficult verse, the pronoun **them** most likely refers to the words and deeds of Yahweh, and the pronoun **they** to people in general, who live because of what Yahweh does. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [upon your words and deeds people live]

17.note: Hezekiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **welfare**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because it was good for me]

Hezekiah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **have loved** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to contrast Yahweh’s wonderful love for him with his previous bitter experience. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But for your part, you have loved my soul]

The word translated as **you have loved** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe copying from dictation may have thought he heard a similar-sounding consonant, resulting in this word. With the other consonant, it would say “you have held back,” which seems to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [you have held back]

Here Hezekiah is speaking of death as if it were **the pit**, a deep hole in the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from death and nonexistence]

Hezekiah is using the possessive form to describe a **pit** that is characterized by **nothingness**, that is, the grave, where there is nothing. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the pit that has nothing in it]

Hezekiah is using **you have thrown all of my sins behind your back** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you have forgiven all of my sins.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have forgiven all of my sins]

18.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

18.q: כִּ֣י לֹ֥א שְׁא֛וֹל תּוֹדֶ֖⁠ךָּ מָ֣וֶת יְהַלְלֶ֑⁠ךָּ
18.note: Hezekiah is speaking of **Sheol** and **death** as if they were living things that could **thank** and **praise** Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For those in Sheol do not thank you, and those who are dead do not praise you]

Here Hezekiah is speaking of people who have died as if they were **the ones going down** into **the pit**, a deep hole representing the grave. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who have died]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how faithful you are]

19.note: Hezekiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, his joy and relief at being among the living rather than the dead. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, those who are alive]

Hezekiah is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Those who are alive, those who are alive]
The pronoun **He** refers to living people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [A living person thanks you]

Hezekiah is not referring to a specific **father**. He means fathers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [fathers make known to sons]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how faithful you are]

20.note: Hezekiah is using the possessive form to describe a **house** that is characterized by **Yahweh**, that is, the temple that belongs to Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the temple where Yahweh is worshiped]

Hezekiah is using a construction in which a verb, **play**, which means “to play stringed instruments,” and its object, **stringed instruments**, come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and we instrumentalize with instruments]

21.note: This word is used here to mark a break in the main story line. This gives background information about Isaiah and Hezekiah. Alternate translation: [At that time,]
The pronoun **them** refers to Hezekiah’s servants. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Let Hezekiah’s servants take]
This was used as a poultice. The meaning of this can be made clear. Alternate translation: [use a poultice of mashed figs]

A **boil** is a kind of painful skin infection. If your readers would not be familiar with what a boil is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the infected skin]

22.note: Hezekiah is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which Yahweh lived. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]
